newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco urges commercial banks to cut interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Morocco urges commercial banks to cut interest rates.

text.p: Morocco's Finance Minister Mohamed Kabbaj on Tuesday urged commercial banks to lower their interest rates to improve the financing of small and medium-sized firms and boost the economy.

Addressing the sixth meeting of National Council of Money and Saving (NCMS), Kabbaj said "the real rate applied to economic operators remains for us a major source of concern...We consider that conditions are now in place for a relaxation of interest rates".
The meeting at Bank al-Maghrib (central bank) headquarters was also attended by governor Mohamed Seqat and Morocco's bankers' association chairman Othman Benjelloun.

Since the liberalisation of interest rates in February 1996 the banks had made no significant efforts "to lower their interest rates while inflation dramatically declined and the Treasury reduced its interest rates three times," Kabbaj said.
Moroccan inflation dropped to 3.0 percent in 1996 from 6.2 percent in 1995 and the treasury cut its rates by a total 1.5 percent during the last 16 months.

"The lowering rates policy, which we are calling for, will be encouraged from our side by a new reduction from 10 to 5.0 percent of the public securities minimum portfolio by end 1997," Kabbaj told the meeting.
The reduction which aimed at boosting the domestic banking system "would be translated by a new decline" of interest rates, he said.
The present interest rate applied by commercial banks stands between a minimum 8.5 to 13.75 percent on short term loans and from 9.0 to 15 percent on long-term loans, a stockbroker said.

Small and medium-sized enterprises, which represent an "essential component of the country's productive system should be encouraged to get a best access" to financial resources on the market, the minister said.

Kabbaj urged the meeting to set up "a working group" inside the NCMS "to establish a clear diagnosis on the present financing conditions of small and medium-sized enterprises and propose measures to improve these conditions".
As part of a long-term plan aimed at upgrading an estimated 4,000 firms, the government devoted 100 million dirhams ($10.5 million) to help the financing of these enterprises, he said.
Kabbaj said discussions were under way with Spain and the European Union "to mobilise more funds" for these enterprises.
"The government efforts cannot meet the target without the involvement of Moroccan banks which should reduce their intermediation margins and grant complementary funds," Kabbaj added.
According to Bank al-Maghrib, loans to the economy rose 36 percent to 3.7 billion dirhams during the first five months of the year compared with same period in 1996.
The loans benefited refining, construction, textile sectors and financing firms.

Benjelloun who spoke on behalf of Moroccan bankers, said the banks already made an effort earlier this year to reduce by one percent interest rate on investment loans "but lowering rates was not the only element which boosts the investment and economic growth...But the banks will meet soon to examine the lowering of rates demanded by the monetary authorities".
